Graduates of the programme should be able to analyse the role of communication and media in processes of social change at individual, organisational and societal level. Based on this analysis, they are able to support the design of relevant communication interventions and strategies. The focus on communication in processes of change means that the BCL programme not only contains courses on theories of communication science and on communication practices and processes, but students are also introduced to relevant theories of the neighbouring social science disciplines social psychology, sociology, political science and public policy. This knowledge allows graduates to understand the role of communication in a broader context of social change and social intervention and leads to more effective designs and technologies in processes of social and organisational change in life-science-related domains.Students specialise in a life science domain of choice e.g. sustainability, health, climate change, natural resource management, urbanisation or food. The unique combination of education in communication science with solid knowledge in a life science domain allows students to explore life sciences issues through the lens of communication.
This enables graduates to bridge the gap between different disciplines as well as between societal stakeholders and contribute to solving pressing societal problems. Education of Communication, Philosophy, Technology and Education

The section Communication, Philosophy, Technology and Education (CPTE) provides education for Bachelor, Master and PhD students of Wageningen UR and other universities. Professionals are also welcome to participate in our education. CPTE offers courses and supervises theses and internships (for WUR students only).

Theses and internships

CPTE supervises Bachelor, Master and PhD students when they work on their thesis or do an internship. You can either develop your own topic or find an internship position on your own. Another way is to select an available internship position or thesis topic provided by CPTE. Please note that your thesis topic must always be approved by your thesis supervisor and the internship position must be approved by the education coordinator. Check the available topics on our Brightspace page (for WUR students only).

Go to Brightspace

Courses

CPTE facilitates more than 50 introductory and advanced courses in various social science and life science programmes. In our education we aim to enhance understanding on the processes that may foster bridging between people that live in different ‘worlds’. In our courses students learn to develop new forms of dialogue and persuasive communication, analyse and clarify key values and arguments, and to contribute to strategies for inclusive development and responsible innovation. Students learn about analytical and practical approaches through real-life cases and experiences. This helps them to become professionals that can link theory and practice, connect different worlds and contribute to change.

Minors

The advanced BSc Minor Communication, Research and Practice deals with several aspects of the relation between scientific research and communication practice. In their future work, many students with a life science or social science background will be confronted with societal responses to research findings, the setting of research agenda’s in support of societal innovation, and the design of communication research as a preparation for communication planning. In this minor students come to grips with the different ways in which communication can relate to research.

The BSc Minor Communication for Change gives students a comprehensive introduction to the interdisciplinary field of applied communication sciences. After a general introduction, the BSc minor offers basic insight in social psychological mechanisms and offers specialised courses to zoom in first on communication and individual change, and later on communication and organisational change.

This BSc minor provides students with an in-depth understanding of multiple social and bio-physical environmental determinants of health, and their interaction at the individual, local and global level. The BSc minor combines expertise from health psychology, social psychology, health promotion, epidemiology and communication. Overall, the BSc minor aims to give students insight into the multiple causes of and solutions for health issues, to understand the interdependence of the causes and teach them how to address problems through health promotion actions, strategic communication and policy.

Philosophy literally means: love of wisdom, but we see it first and foremost as asking and exploring very basic questions: about what knowledge is and how to attain it, about our relationship to the world, and about how we should live. In philosophy, it is common to ask questions about things we normally just take for granted. Does the world exist? Can we trust our senses? Can we have knowledge about what is right or wrong? What is happiness? It is a bit like children who can continue asking "why is that so?" This might sound silly sometimes, but it can also lead to new insights. Wisdom is maybe not to know a lot, but, much more, to be aware of the limitations of what one can know. And we can find those limits only by continuing to ask questions.

Philosophy is not always abstract and theoretical, it can be very practical. For example when we try to to give good ethical reasons for choices we should make, in policy or in private life. Can it be justified for the government to require parents to have their children vaccinated? Is it right to kill animals for food? Do we have obligations to future generations, if it comes to reducing climate change? These questions require careful reflection and analysis. But they also raise deep controversies and conflicting views. Can systematic thinking help overcoming such conflicts?

In the minor we do not only study and discuss ethical and philosophical themes. We also practice specific ways of reasoning, with the aim to develop skills in critical thinking. This includes, for example, argumentation analysis and thought experiments, but also specific forms of deliberation, such as Socratic dialogue. Students interested in philosophy or applied ethics can deepen their skills in critical reflection, acquire a broader understanding of philosophical traditions, and engage in ethical analysis of societal problems in the Wageningen domain that (includes but also) goes beyond the specific domain of their own study program.

The course is set up as an inquiry into the life science domains of Wageningen University, with the aim that students learn both about what those life sciences entail, as well as their personal preferences for certain life science domains. By doing so, students are introduced to key concepts and research problems in the life sciences, and at the same time get a basic understanding of complex societal issues in life-science related domains. In addition, by using models and theories from science communication, it surveys dominant as well as alternative ways of communicating science and technology related to societal change (or resistance to change). The course concentrates on six domains: health, food, urbanisation, climate, nature, and sustainability. At the end of the course, students will be able to make an informed choice which of the six domains to select as their focus area ('track') in subsequent courses and in their BSc thesis.

This course consists of lectures; writing a group assignment; studying literature; and writing an individual essay. Through these activities, students explore their preferences for specific life science domains, while at the same time they learn about those life sciences through their explorations. The communication issues and challenges within each life sciences domain present the central focus. Students learn about what life sciences are being studied and taught in Wageningen, using the list of over 30 minors that they can choose from. During the group assignment, each group will write three chapters, each one on a different Wageningen life science domain. For each chapter, the group will identify a Wageningen scientist, and an article written by that scientist. The life science article will form the foundation for a short interview with the scientist, and focuses on the communication issues related to their scientific work. The chapter will take the form of a ‘feature’ article and report the findings as a popular-science article. Students will inform each other of their work and views through presentations.

In this course, we unravel the processes of polarization and the role that communication can play in exacerbating societal divisions. Additionally, we explore how various actors can use communication to depolarize. Specifically, our focus is on life science themes such as climate change, sustainability, and health.

We discuss various forms of polarization, including ideological, affective, and factual belief polarization, and assess the extent of polarization in these themes. We then investigate how communication content plays a role in polarization processes. This involves examining the polarization of content in (social) media, such as in the climate debate. We also explore how exposure to misinformation and disinformation (e.g., during the COVID-19 crisis) contributes to growing divides among population groups. Related phenomena like politicization, where political actors become more prominent in public discourse at the expense of scientists, are also addressed.

In the first weeks, we focus on key insights into polarization and depolarization and the role of communication in these processes. Subsequently, we delve into applications on specific life science themes, namely climate change, sustainability, and health. Special attention is given to understanding theories and empirical findings described in scientific publications. These are discussed weekly in lectures where students actively engage in discussions and presentations.

During workshops, students work on a group assignment, which revolves around how communication can (de)polarization, based on insights from literature, practical experiences, and a small empirical study (e.g., interviews or a small experiment).

This course familiarizes students with how communication can contribute to addressing urgent life science challenges. Furthermore, they apply acquired knowledge, conduct research, and learn how scientific research can be applied. This enables them to integrate practical applications with scientific insights and create innovative solutions.

and knowledge play an important role in how societal problems and challenges are defined and addressed. Knowledge from the life-sciences is often translated into technical innovations that are supposed to help address climate change, malnutrition or environmental pollution. Often, social innovations (such as new regulations, policies, processes or organizational models) are also needed to address societal problems and/or ensure that technical solutions become effective. Communication plays an important role in the process of developing effective technical and social innovations, and also in reaching agreement about their use in society, and in processes of diffusion and scaling.
In this course, you develop a theoretical and practical understanding of the interplay between communication, knowledge and change, drawing on insights from communication science, science, technology and innovation studies and the sociology of knowledge. CPT18306 Global Challenges and Communication in a Changing World, or CPT28806 Introduction to Communication and Technology in Rural Innovation and Development

","type":{"code":"AK","id":"AK","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Assumed knowledge on:"}],"uid":"fdda01e3-c543-4b24-a3cb-9c4690e5a654"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

Public policies are the outcome of political processes in which communication plays an important role. For example, government organisations; local and online communities; interest groups such as those of industrialists; civil society organisations such as environmental organisations and movements, experts; media and the broader public – all these engage in communication to shape and influence public policy. This happens through many different forms of interaction. Think, for example, of lobbying, public debate, and participatory approaches in development. From a communication perspective, policymaking is then a continuous, complex negotiation about meaning making that defines what counts as an important public issue (agenda setting processes), who is able to put forward their identification of problems and solutions (framing) and what interaction processes can look like.
Power and politics express themselves in many ways here. Key questions in this course are: how can the roles of different types of actors be understood? Who gets to speak and be heard, and why? How can inclusions and exclusions be understood? What forms of communication advance inclusion and decrease polarization? What are the potential threats of disinformation for politics and policy? This course provides a broad foundation for understanding different roles of communication in the making of public policy, and for helping to advance inclusive governance through communication. The course is structured as a hands-on roleplay, with student groups taking the roles of think tanks. These think tanks advise governments and other stakeholders, and inform public debate, on communication around political issues in the domains of environment, international development and health.

Sustainability is one of the most intractable, daunting and ‘wicked’ challenges of our generation. It is ‘wicked’ because it has multiple interrelated causes and no simple solution. Radical transformations need to address not only the multiple roots of wicked problems but crucially to engage citizens to create system change. But how?

We provide students with concepts and methods to explore the challenge of communicating sustainability responsibly. Across content lectures, we examine the universalising planetary boundaries framework that defines a 'safe operating space' for humanity and one that relies on a ‘deficit’ model of citizen engagement. Following critique, we explore approaches aimed at empowering, democratising, embedding, decolonising and popularising communication practices for sustainability.

To gain hands-on research experience, students develop a focus group project on a 'wicked' sustainability challenge of their own choice recruiting fellow WUR students as participants. Learning and developing skills of focus group design, active listening, small group moderation and analysis we explore how the views and values of citizens can co-produce new approaches for communicating sustainability.

This intensive course provides insight into theoretical and practical-strategic matters of risk communication. Special attention will be given to risk communication in the context of the life sciences issues and life science technologies such as malaria, zoonoses, gene technology, flooding, climate change, novel agrotechnologies, and food scares. Key questions in these contexts are: Is vaccination safe for children? What are hazards of nuclear energy, fracking, and the use of nitrogen-based fertilizers in agriculture? How high are flood risks in the Netherlands, and how are these risks associated to climate change? These questions have significant implications for the lives of many people, for political decision-making, and for industry stakeholders, for example. Communication – be it in traditional mass media, on digital platforms, or in private life – shapes the formation of these implications considerably: Public engagement with a range of environmental, health, and technology issues and the risks associated with them is mediated through journalism, political campaigns, advertising, for example. This course provides insight into theory, empirical research, and practice of risk communication in our networked, digitalized, knowledge-based, “post-normal” society.

Special attention is dedicated to risk related to life science topics like climate change, food (production), zoonoses, water management, biotechnology, and genomics. We will discuss psychological theories regarding risk and uncertainty perception. How do people process complex information regarding particular risks and what is the role of emotions therein? How does media coverage of risks affect the public’s sense of anxiety? We will also discuss sociological theories of risk and trust. Is there a general mistrust of science and technology or a lack of knowledge about hazardous science and technology issues? Under what conditions are institutions capable and willing of handling and communicating risks?

During the course, students will work on a group project about a risk of choice. For this risk, students will do a stakeholder analysis, analyse stakeholder perceptions, provide an overview of relevant communications and analyse these communications in order to develop to recommendations for effective risk communication based on theories from the course.

CPT39003 Thesis Path Communication and Life Sciences","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"The course aims to provide an in-depth overview of various research methods that communication scientists may apply to study societal issues. During the course, students acquire research skills that are necessary for the independent conduct of research. The combination of methodological reflection and practical exercises enables critical reflection on the potential effects and limitations of various approaches to data collection and analysis, and on the relationship between theoretical perspectives, research problems and methodological choices.

Specific attention is paid to: 1. choosing research approaches and designs, based on the underlying research premises and the research question at hand; 2. applying various methods, techniques and tools for data collection; and 3. using subsequent procedures for data analysis and processing. Within these three skill areas, both quantitative and qualitative approaches will be taught. Quantitative methods include survey methods and experiments. Qualitative methods include interviews and focus groups. This course provides a mix of traditional and innovative methods, techniques and tools, both quantitative and qualitative, applied in communication research. Research skills are built through an active learning process consisting of exemplary cases of research practices, and supervised practicals (individual and group), including tutorials allowing students to become acquainted with the practice of quantitative and qualitative data analysis. Finally, the group assignment focuses on acquiring skills to critically describe, analyze and assess research methods of scientific studies. This also entails learning how to read and understand scientific articles, which is a basic part of the scientific endeavor.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"The course employs different types of learning activities:
  • Lectures, based on problem-oriented case studies: concrete research problems are used to illustrate how different research methods, techniques and tools can be used.
  • Practicals including collecting and analyzing data.
  • Literature study of textbook chapter(s) and scientific paper(s) in preparation of the lectures, practicals and exam.
  • Group assignment: in groups of two, students will write three chapters in which the practicals of each week will be described in a Methods-type format.
  • Reading assignments to further learn how to analytically read empirical scientific papers.

","type":{"code":"AK","id":"AK","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Assumed knowledge on:"}],"uid":"fdda01e3-c543-4b24-a3cb-9c4690e5a654"}},{"language":"EN","text":"\"Media Society and Politics\" familiarises students with the role of media in social, cultural, political, and economic life, with an additional focus on the increasing intertwining of digital media technology with our daily lives. Society is heavily mediated, and media influence both how people think, form attitudes, and behave, as well as play a significant role in the political decision-making process. The overall aim of the course is to gain a profound understanding of the interactions between politicians, journalists, and citizens and to be able to apply these insights in an original way to a relevant case in the life science domain.
The course examines both traditional and digital media, with attention to historical roots so that students build a solid foundation that can be applied to contemporary developments. In the first three weeks, we critically assess the (still influential?) role of traditional media. Afterward, we shift our focus to digital media and technological innovations shaping society on a daily basis.
Overview of themes per week:
Week 1: Introduction, focus on interactions between media and the public (agenda setting, priming, framing), process tracing.
Week 2: Interactions between politics and media (indexing, news selection, journalistic norms, and role perceptions).
Week 3: Interactions between politics and the public (representation, responsiveness, policy formation).
Week 4: Integration, changes due to digitization and politicisation.
This course provides students with an in-depth exploration of the complex relationships between media, society, and politics, building on insights briefly covered in previous courses, particularly Communication Science. It offers students a solid foundational knowledge of media (both traditional and digital) in all its aspects. The course emphasises both the theories underlying media research and their application and linkage to new developments in our (digital) media society.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

In this course, we explore organisations' ways of communicating strategically with their environment. Focus is on what communication can contribute to an adequate orientation of an organisation to an ever-changing environment. We zoom in on challenges connected with organizational responsibilities in society, considering life-science related themes like health, food and the environment. Externally, organisations have to know what is going on, they must present themselves to a wide range of stakeholders and manage their reputation. These challenges have become increasingly difficult in situations where, due to digitalization and mediatization, information spreads quickly and organizations are under constant scrutiny of NGOs, the general public and other interested parties. Internally, organisations need to accept change as a basic mechanism for staying “in tune”, but at the same time keep employees committed. We explore and discuss currently relevant themes in this context, supported by various theoretical perspectives and a range of case materials. How can we conceptualize the way organisations can relate to their environment? How do organizations influence stakeholder perceptions, and handle tensions that often emerge? How to relate, for example, to polarization and conflicts between stakeholder expectations? How to take responsibility, for example when it comes to environmental impact of what you do, and communicate about that? How to communicate when there is a crisis and reputation is under threat? We study how organizations can act strategically in these matters, exploring different theoretical approaches and the application of such approaches to the analysis of real-life organisational communication challenges and strategic decision making with regard to communication. We also consider ethical dimensions, given tensions that often emerge between taking responsibility for impacts on stakeholders and the environment, and organisational strategies.

Students are encouraged to share knowledge and skills that they have acquired in the BCL programme. And to integrate these theories, methods, and approaches related to both communication sciences as well as the selected life science domain, in their own thesis project. The thesis project itself is part of the course ‘BSc Thesis Communication and Life Sciences (CPT82315)’.
In order to integrate previously acquired knowledge, students are stimulated to reflect upon and share their past experiences. They identify the steps within a research project, such as: how to define a research theme and a research gap, how to find and use literature, how to formulate appropriate research questions, what research is required to answer the research questions, how to use a theoretical or conceptual framework for their research, and how to select research methods and a set up that fits with the research questions. In addition, students reflect upon the skills that are necessary to write a thesis such as planning, scientific writing and communication with a thesis supervisor.
Unique in the BCL study programme is the combination of both communication courses and courses in a particular life science domain. In this course, students experience boundary crossing by exchanging experiences about the different life science domains. Moreover they reflect on boundary crossing between communication and their selected life science domain, and how they can apply this in their thesis.
Students participate in thesis rings that are established during the course and will continue during thesis writing. The thesis ring has two main functions: providing an opportunity to give and receive peer feedback, and to provide social support. The course’s main focus is on developing students’ presentation skills, with specific attention to how a message is delivered beyond its content. The course provides a starting point from which students gain initial insight into their current presentation abilities, creating a baseline for further practice. Students begin at their own level of competence and take their first steps towards strengthening their presentation skills by working on personal development goals. Throughout the course, students develop their observation skills by observing their own and others’ presentations, which supports their self-awareness by identifying strengths, areas for growth, evaluating progress, and determining next steps. In parallel, this approach helps students build the skills needed to continue improving their presentation abilities independently after the course and at their own pace. While this process is embedded in presentation practice, it also helps students develop transferable skills that support their broader academic and personal development. Peer interaction and peer feedback further enhance this learning process.

","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

The course consists of approximately 10 contact hours spread across four sessions. During these sessions, students actively work on developing their presentation skills through individual and group presentation exercises, observing their peers, exchanging (peer) feedback and and engaging in guided self-evaluation based on observation. In the plenary part presentation techniques and effective delivery strategies are discussed, demonstrated, and practiced, and in the second half of the sessions students actively practice their presentation skills to a small audience of peers. These presentations are recorded and used by students to observe their own performance, increase their self-awareness, and identify points for improvement.

The remaining 18-hours are reserved for self-study activities including: preparing and rehearsing presentations, engaging with relevant materials (readings, observing and analyzing videos) and self-evaluation tasks.

Attendance at all four sessions is required, as the course builds on previous sessions, during which students depend on one another for observations, (peer)feedback and collaborative learning. Active participation and consistent presence are therefore essential for achieving the intended learning outcomes.

PAP30806 Governance and Policy Change.","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"
  • This course introduces communication students to the scholarly realm of public administration and policy. Public administration and policy scholars analyze how the world of public governance functions and develop suggestions to strengthen governance in the network society. Knowledge about public governance is essential to communication students, because: (i) governance is about how societies deal with perceived problems and as such shapes everyday actions and institutions, (ii) ideas and (political) communication play a big role in how public and private actors frame societal problems and possible solutions within governance networks, and (iii) governments and other actors are both important sources and objects of communication.
  • During the course, students will explore different aspects of public administration and policy about public governance, including the role of ideas and communication herein. To this end, the course will consist of two interconnected learning streams:
    students will engage in-depth with one seminal example of scholarly work from the field by reading a classic book, discussing this work and reflecting on its links to political events and processes in small reading groups;
  • During the lectures, a broad overview of foundational concepts and ideas in the study of public administration will be explored, providing students with the skills to navigate the field and to approach governance questions in a scientifically sound manner. These will further give students the chance to contextualize the classics in relation to broader ideational currents in the field, as well as to contemporary issues relevant to the life sciences.
  • The course ends with an excursion to The Hague, where students will experience practical applications of the key ideas learned in the course in learning activities involving political practitioners.
  • Participation in the course does not require any previous knowledge, but the courses welcomes every student who wants to learn more about public governance and the ways in which political decision making function.

Note: This course can not be combined in an individual programme with HSO11305 Sociology of Health.

The course consists of lectures of two hours two times a week, and tutorials of two hours one time a week. Attendance of the tutorials is mandatory as well as the portfolio work and weekly assignments that serve as preparation. In the weekly assignments, students read and analyse a scientific article and respond to a number of questions in writing. In the portfolio, based on a media clip (audio, video or a combination), students link a theme of their choice to the main thinkers of the course. The lectures discuss fundamental sociological questions and themes. During the tutorials the articles are discussed in which fundamental sociological insights are applied to the context of international development and communication. Furthermore, discussing the weekly assignments and engagement in exercises relate the topic of the article to the life world of the students. Both early as well as contemporary sociologists are discussed. We will discuss their insights and assess their influence on sociological analyses of contemporary societal issues.

communication, we cannot achieve the necessary changes in issues, such as sustainability and health. “

In this course, we examine how people become informed about societal issues and how they are influenced by the abundance of information that reaches them in various ways. We pay special attention to (social) media, how reporting on life science topics comes about, and the role that such reporting plays in policy-making processes.

We address many urgent and important questions and answer them using central, new, and established concepts and theories from communication science and related disciplines such as social psychology. For example, we explore questions like: How do we inform ourselves in our daily lives? How does communication influence us? Why is media attention important? How is news created? How do influencers influence us? How do media contribute to inequality? What are the consequences of our digital media use? The theories we discuss include Agenda-setting theory, Framing, and Two-step flow theory.

This course establishes the foundation for communication scientific thinking, where fundamental theories are directly applied to current issues based on recent scientific insights. These insights are applied to topics central to Wageningen, such as climate change, sustainability, health, and nutrition. The course is set up as an inquiry into the life science domains of Wageningen University, with the aim that students learn both about what those life sciences entail, as well as their personal preferences for certain life science domains. By doing so, students are introduced to key concepts and research problems in the life sciences, and at the same time get a basic understanding of complex societal issues in life-science related domains. In addition, by using models and theories from science communication, it surveys dominant as well as alternative ways of communicating science and technology related to societal change (or resistance to change). The course concentrates on six domains: health, food, urbanisation, climate, nature, and sustainability. At the end of the course, students will be able to make an informed choice which of the six domains to select as their focus area ('track') in subsequent courses and in their BSc thesis.

","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

This course consists of lectures; writing a group assignment; studying literature; and writing an individual essay. Through these activities, students explore their preferences for specific life science domains, while at the same time they learn about those life sciences through their explorations. The communication issues and challenges within each life sciences domain present the central focus. Students learn about what life sciences are being studied and taught in Wageningen, using the list of over 30 minors that they can choose from. During the group assignment, each group will write three chapters, each one on a different Wageningen life science domain. For each chapter, the group will identify a Wageningen scientist, and an article written by that scientist. The life science article will form the foundation for a short interview with the scientist, and focuses on the communication issues related to their scientific work. The chapter will take the form of a ‘feature’ article and report the findings as a popular-science article. Students will inform each other of their work and views through presentations.

Students have a central role during these sessions: they do short presentation assignments themselves and provide each other feedback. Students present in each session for a live audience. In this course, we unravel the processes of polarization and the role that communication can play in exacerbating societal divisions. Additionally, we explore how various actors can use communication to depolarize. Specifically, our focus is on life science themes such as climate change, sustainability, and health.

We discuss various forms of polarization, including ideological, affective, and factual belief polarization, and assess the extent of polarization in these themes. We then investigate how communication content plays a role in polarization processes. This involves examining the polarization of content in (social) media, such as in the climate debate. We also explore how exposure to misinformation and disinformation (e.g., during the COVID-19 crisis) contributes to growing divides among population groups. Related phenomena like politicization, where political actors become more prominent in public discourse at the expense of scientists, are also addressed.

In the first weeks, we focus on key insights into polarization and depolarization and the role of communication in these processes. Subsequently, we delve into applications on specific life science themes, namely climate change, sustainability, and health. Special attention is given to understanding theories and empirical findings described in scientific publications. These are discussed weekly in lectures where students actively engage in discussions and presentations.

During workshops, students work on a group assignment, which revolves around how communication can (de)polarization, based on insights from literature, practical experiences, and a small empirical study (e.g., interviews or a small experiment).

This course familiarizes students with how communication can contribute to addressing urgent life science challenges. Furthermore, they apply acquired knowledge, conduct research, and learn how scientific research can be applied. This enables them to integrate practical applications with scientific insights and create innovative solutions.

For example, parliamentarians; government organisations; local and online communities; interest groups such as those of industrialists; civil society organisations such as environmental organisations; experts; media and the broader public – all these engage in communication to shape and influence public policy. This happens through many different forms of interaction. Think, for example, of lobbying, public debate, and participatory approaches in development. From a communication perspective, policymaking is then a continuous, complex negotiation about meaning making that defines what counts as an important public issue (agenda setting processes), who can speak and be heard, and who is able to successfully put forward their identification of problems and solutions (framing).
Power and politics express themselves in many ways here. Key questions in this course are: how can the roles of different types of actors be understood? Who gets to speak and be heard, and why? How can inclusions and exclusions be understood? What forms of communication advance inclusion and decrease polarization? What are the potential threats of disinformation for politics and policy? This course provides a broad foundation for understanding different roles of communication in the making of public policy, and for helping to advance inclusive governance through communication. The course is structured as a role-play, with student groups taking the roles of consultants advising government on communication in the context of a self-selected policy process in a life science context (with options provided in the domains of health, environment and international development).","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"- lectures;

Sustainability is one of the most intractable, daunting and ‘wicked’ challenges of our generation. It is ‘wicked’ because it has multiple interrelated causes and no simple solution. Radical transformations need to address not only the multiple roots of wicked problems but crucially to engage citizens to create system change. But how?

We provide students with concepts and methods to explore the challenge of communicating sustainability responsibly. Across content lectures, we examine two dominant and interconnected approaches: a planetary boundaries framework that seeks to define a 'safe operating space' for humanity and an information ‘deficit’ model to science communication that seeks to define a mode of citizen engagement. Following critique, we explore approaches aimed at engaging, visioning, empowering, politicising, embedding and pluralising communication practices.

To gain hands-on research experience, students develop a focus group project on a “wicked” sustainability challenge of their own choice recruiting fellow WUR students as participants. Learning and practising skills of focus group design, active listening, small group moderation and analysis we explore how the views and values of citizens can co-produce new approaches for communicating sustainability.

In our rapidly changing knowledge society, experts and non-experts tend to have different appreciations of science and technology issues. What exactly is the nature of these differences and what are the communicative implications? We will discuss psychological theories regarding risk perception. How do people process complex information regarding particular risks and what is the role of emotions therein? How does media coverage of risks affect the public's sense of anxiety? Attention will also be paid to sociological theories of risk and trust. Is there a general mistrust of science and technology, and can this be explained by a trust or knowledge deficit of the public? Under what conditions are institutions capable of handling and communicating risks? CPT39003 Thesis Path Communication and Life Sciences","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"The course aims to provide an in-depth overview of various research methods that communication scientists may apply to study societal issues. During the course, students acquire research skills that are necessary for the independent conduct of research. The combination of methodological reflection and practical exercises enables critical reflection on the potential effects and limitations of various approaches to data collection and analysis, and on the relationship between theoretical perspectives, research problems and methodological choices.

Specific attention is paid to: 1. choosing research approaches and designs, based on the underlying research premises and the research question at hand; 2. applying various methods, techniques and tools for data collection; and 3. using subsequent procedures for data analysis and processing. Within these three skill areas, both quantitative and qualitative approaches will be taught. Quantitative methods include survey methods and experiments. Qualitative methods include interviews and focus groups. This course provides a mix of traditional and innovative methods, techniques and tools, both quantitative and qualitative, applied in communication research. Research skills are built through an active learning process consisting of exemplary cases of research practices, and supervised practicals (individual and group), including tutorials allowing students to become acquainted with the practice of quantitative and qualitative data analysis. Finally, the group assignment focuses on acquiring skills to critically describe, analyze and assess research methods of scientific studies. This also entails learning how to read and understand scientific articles, which is a basic part of the scientific endeavor.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"The course employs different types of learning activities:
  • Lectures, based on problem-oriented case studies: concrete research problems are used to illustrate how different research methods, techniques and tools can be used.
  • Practicals including collecting and analyzing data.
  • Literature study of textbook chapter(s) and scientific paper(s) in preparation of the lectures, practicals and exam.
  • Group assignment: in groups of two, students will write three chapters in which the practicals of each week will be described in a Methods-type format.
  • Reading assignments to further learn how to analytically read empirical scientific papers.

on:"}],"uid":"fdda01e3-c543-4b24-a3cb-9c4690e5a654"}},{"language":"EN","text":"\"Media Society and Politics\" familiarises students with the role of media in social, cultural, political, and economic life, with an additional focus on the increasing intertwining of digital media technology with our daily lives. Society is heavily mediated, and media influence both how people think, form attitudes, and behave, as well as play a significant role in the political decision-making process. The overall aim of the course is to gain a profound understanding of the interactions between politicians, journalists, and citizens and to be able to apply these insights in an original way to a relevant case in the life science domain.
The course examines both traditional and digital media, with attention to historical roots so that students build a solid foundation that can be applied to contemporary developments. In the first three weeks, we critically assess the (still influential?) role of traditional media. Afterward, we shift our focus to digital media and technological innovations shaping society on a daily basis.
Overview of themes per week:
Week 1: Introduction, focus on interactions between media and the public (agenda setting, priming, framing), process tracing.
Week 2: Interactions between politics and media (indexing, news selection, journalistic norms, and role perceptions).
Week 3: Interactions between politics and the public (representation, responsiveness, policy formation).
Week 4: Integration, changes due to digitization and politicisation.
This course provides students with an in-depth exploration of the complex relationships between media, society, and politics, building on insights briefly covered in previous courses, particularly Communication Science. It offers students a solid foundational knowledge of media (both traditional and digital) in all its aspects. The course emphasises both the theories underlying media research and their application and linkage to new developments in our (digital) media society.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

internal communication. Externally, organisations have to know what is going on, they must present themselves to a wide range of stakeholders and manage their reputation. These challenges have become increasingly difficult in sitiuations where due to digitalization and mediatization information spreads quickly and organizations are under constant scrutiny of journalists, the general public and other interested parties. Internally, organisations need to accept change as a basic mechanism for staying “in tune”, but at the same time keep employees committed. The question is what communication can contribute to an adequate orientation of an organisation on an environment that continuously changes. We explore and discuss currently relevant themes in this context, supported by various theoretical perspectives and a range of case materials. Why and how do organisations communicate about their goals and ideas? What channels do they use and how do they make strategic decisions? How do interactions with stakeholders impact an organisation’s reputation? What does relating to the environment mean for an organisation’s identity – members’ own ideas about what the organisation stands for? How do organisations communicate about their social responsibility in a context where polarization is an ever-present threat, and why? How can they communicate when there is a crisis and their reputation is under threat? We study how organizations can act strategically in these matters, exploring different theoretical approaches as also the application of such approaches to the analysis of real-life organisational communication challenges and strategic decision making with regard to communication.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

Students are encouraged to share knowledge and skills that they have acquired in the BCL programme. And to integrate these theories, methods, and approaches related to both communication sciences as well as the selected life science domain, in their own thesis project. The thesis project itself is part of the course ‘BSc Thesis Communication and Life Sciences (CPT82315)’.
In order to integrate previously acquired knowledge, students are stimulated to reflect upon and share their past experiences. They identify the steps within a research project, such as: how to define a research theme and a research gap, how to find and use literature, how to formulate appropriate research questions, what research is required to answer the research questions, how to use a theoretical or conceptual framework for their research, and how to select research methods and a set up that fits with the research questions. In addition, students reflect upon the skills that are necessary to write a thesis such as planning, scientific writing and communication with a thesis supervisor.
Unique in the BCL study programme is the combination of both communication courses and courses in a particular life science domain. In this course, students experience boundary crossing by exchanging experiences about the different life science domains. Moreover they reflect on boundary crossing between communication and their selected life science domain, and how they can apply this in their thesis.
Students participate in thesis rings that are established during the course and will continue during thesis writing. The thesis ring has two main functions: providing an opportunity to give and receive peer feedback, and to provide social support.   • This course introduces communication students to the scholarly realm of public administration and policy. Public administration and policy scholars analyze how the world of public governance functions and develop suggestions to strengthen governance in the network society. Knowledge about public governance is essential to communication students, because: (i) governance is about how societies deal with perceived problems and as such shapes everyday actions and institutions, (ii) ideas and (political) communication play a big role in how public and private actors frame societal problems and possible solutions within governance networks, and (iii) governments and other actors are both important sources and objects of communication.
  • During the course, students will explore different aspects of public administration and policy about public governance, including the role of ideas and communication herein. To this end, the course will consist of two interconnected learning streams:
    students will engage in-depth with one seminal example of scholarly work from the field by reading a classic book, discussing this work and reflecting on its links to political events and processes in small reading groups;
  • During the lectures, a broad overview of foundational concepts and ideas in the study of public administration will be explored, providing students with the skills to navigate the field and to approach governance questions in a scientifically sound manner. These will further give students the chance to contextualize the classics in relation to broader ideational currents in the field, as well as to contemporary issues relevant to the life sciences.
  • The course ends with an excursion to The Hague, where students will experience practical applications of the key ideas learned in the course in learning activities involving political practitioners.
  • Participation in the course does not require any previous knowledge, but the courses welcomes every student who wants to learn more about public governance and the ways in which political decision making function.

Note: This course can not be combined in an individual programme with HSO11305 Sociology of Health.

The course consists of lectures of two hours two times a week, and tutorials of two hours one time a week. Attendance of the tutorials is mandatory as well as the portfolio work and weekly assignments that serve as preparation. In the weekly assignments, students read and analyse a scientific article and respond to a number of questions in writing. In the portfolio, based on a media clip (audio, video or a combination), students link a theme of their choice to the main thinkers of the course. The lectures discuss fundamental sociological questions and themes. During the tutorials the articles are discussed in which fundamental sociological insights are applied to the context of international development and communication. Furthermore, discussing the weekly assignments and engagement in exercises relate the topic of the article to the life world of the students. Specific attention will be devoted to the early sociologists. We will discuss their insights and assess their influence on more recent sociological analyses of contemporary societal issues.

Minors

Following a minor at the university will deepen your knowledge and competences within a field of the life, social or environmental sciences.

Continue to

  • New minors 2026-2027

What is a minor?

Info about a minor

A minor is a package of courses that have coherence and profundity. They are scheduled in half a year, either in the first or in the second semester of the academic year. Bachelor's minors consist of a cluster of courses of 24 ECTS. When you need to fill up to 30 ECTS, you can choose a WUR course to complement your minor. 

There are thematic minors and programme minors. Thematic minors deal with a specific theme and are multi disciplinary. Programme minors are part of WUR bachelor's majors and might give you admission to a master's programme. If you want that, please check with the study advisor of that MSc.

Please talk to you study advisor or SLB'er about your interests and ambitions before you choose a minor, also to prevent an overlap in your programme.

New minors in the study year 2026-2027

New minors 2026-2027

BioNanoTechnology: in Life, Plant&AgroFood

Nanomaterials are ubiquitously used, from corona tests to microelectronics, from self-healing materials to drug delivery.
Understanding nanomaterials and their interactions with bio-(macro)molecules is important for exploring innovative applications and for understanding potential risks, such as toxicological aspects.

In this minor you will become acquainted with the innovative translational aspects of nanotechnology into real-life applications. 

More about this minor

Decolonizing Science and Development

Debates on decolonizing science and development have gained prominence worldwide. In this minor you will be introduced to multiple meanings of decolonization, including critiques of Eurocentric assumptions in science and development, attention to marginalized and historically oppressed knowledge, and proposals for more inclusive or contextually grounded approaches. 

By bringing together a coherent set of courses, you develop historically grounded, analytically rigorous and socially engaged understandings of these issues.

More about this minor

Biosystems Engineering

This preparation minor for the MSc Biosystems Engineering teaches you a solid mathematical understanding of systems that are dynamic or change over time. One course focuses on the mathematics behind decision science. In addition, you will learn advanced statistical methods needed for research in this complex environment. 

Based on your background, you have a choice to take an introductory course to learn programming in Python if you have little to no experience in programming. Or you can choose two courses that focus on different types of mathematics in the food production sector, namely modelling of time-dependent systems such as bioreactors and an introduction to business economics.

How to apply for a minor

Apply

Before taking a minor, we recommend you to discuss your choices with your study adviser. When you have made your decision, you can register for the minor courses separately like you do for all other courses. When you ask for approval of your entire programme in Osiris, you can add the title of your minor.

External students, from hbo or other Dutch universities, can follow their minor (courses) as a 'bijvakstudent', giving them the right to follow courses at WUR at no extra costs. 

When you are a student from TU/e or Utrecht University, you might also be able to enroll via eduXchange, making registrations easier. Please check their website if your courses are offered here.

International students from partner universities of the Erasmus network have the possibility to take part in exchange programmes and follow a BSc minor at Wageningen University & Research this way.

There are also possibilities for students from non-EU partner universities of Wageningen University & Research, and for students from universities with contacts at Wageningen University & Research in their own area of research. Information can be found on the page for future exchange students.

Students that want to take a minor to prepare for an MSc programme at Wageningen University & Research should contact the study adviser of this MSc programme for information on the possibility of a pre-master programme and/or minor. You can find the contact details of the study advisers on the websites of the MSc programmes.

If you are not registered at a Dutch university or hbo or a partner university there are other ways to register. You can register as a 'contract student'. For registration as a contract student, a fee is charged which is based on the number of ECTS credit points per subject. For a whole minor this could be over € 7000 for non- WUR alumni. Details can be found here.

Student Service Centre provides information for students about admission, registration, tuition fees, legal residence, etc. For more information please check: Student Service Centre.


Add up to 30 ECTS

More info

When you have to follow 30 ECTS for your programme, you have to pick an extra course during your minor. There is room for that. You have room to follow 12 ECTS in periods 1 and 2 and 6 ECTS in period 3. For the second semester it is 12 ECTS in period 5 and 6 and 6 EC in period 4.

It depends on the minor whether this supplementary course can be picked from the Restricted Optionals in the same minor or that you have to pick a different course from the online WUR study handbook.

Always register for seperate courses, also in case of a minor

Although a minor is a coherent package of courses, all students, both external and WUR students, have to register for all the courses seperately, you don't register for a minor in total. You can register for the courses in Osiris once you have received your WUR account after you have applied for 'bijvakstudent'.

You don't need permission form WUR to follow a minor, but it is recommended to discuss your plans with your own study advisor or exam board first. Also, check the course descriptions in the study handbook to see if there is any previous knowledge needed.

Use this 'step by step form' to help you pick and schedule your courses.

Contact us

Strategic Communication, led by chairholder Rens Vliegenthart, studies the dynamics and consequences of communication by (digital) media, political actors, organizations and citizens. Focusing on the processes through which public images, discourses, opinions and behaviour come about and have a keen interest in communication challenges related to life science issues such as climate change, sustainability and health.

Our research

Our research

The strategic communication group investigates the role of communication in a high-choice, digitalised information environment. It has a key interest in societal issues and challenges in the realm of life sciences, such as climate, biodiversity, health, and food security and with a special focus on citizen engagement and (political) participation.

Our research relates to, and integrates four key themes:

  • Sustainability communication
  • Science communication
  • Digitalisation and society
  • Polarisation and dialogue

Education by Strategic Communication

Our courses, including theses and internships, can be followed separately, or as structured part of various educational programmes. Our professors and lecturers supervise many students during their internship, thesis, and PhD projects as well.

Publications & Projects

Publications & Projects

We conduct research to fundamentally understand the use, content, and effects of communication. We want to use this knowledge to have an impact on and change society for the better. This implies that we engage with multiple societal and policy actors during and after our research, with the aim to contribute to a more just, sustainable and equitable society. We devote substantial effort to the valorisation of our findings.

Highlighted projects

  • Redefining the role of the consumer in the transition towards biodiversity-enhancing food systems.
  • The mobilization of political dissatisfaction: causes, content, and consequences
  • Digital Political Communication (focusing on processing)

  • Breaking free from linear assumptions: Unravelling the relationship between affective polarization and democratic support
  • Discourse, framing and narrative: three ways of doing critical, interpretive policy analysis

Chairholder

Rens Vliegenthart has been a professor and chair holder of Strategic Communication at WUR since July 2022. His research focuses on media content and effects, both on citizens and public opinion, as well as on politicians and political decision-making. Rens is specialized in (computer-based) content analysis and time series analysis.
